citation: Behm DG, Granacher U, Warneke K, Aragão-Santos JC, Da Silva-Grigoletto ME, Konrad A (2024). Minimalist Training: Is Lower Dosage or Intensity Resistance Training Effective to Improve Physical Fitness? A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine.
population: Sedentary individuals, resistance training beginners, and untrained adults (including young adult males, untrained women, youth soccer players, pubescent male baseball players)
intervention: Minimalist resistance training protocols: 1 weekly session, <3 sets per exercise, loads below 50% 1RM (range 30-80% 1RM), 6-15 repetitions per set, using multi-joint functional movements
summary: This narrative review examines minimal-dose resistance training for sedentary individuals and beginners. Evidence suggests that a single weekly session with less than three sets per multi-joint exercise at intensities below 50% of 1RM can produce significant strength and hypertrophy gains for at least 8-12 weeks. Multi-joint exercises yield similar or greater effects than single-joint exercises, though the optimal repetition endpoint (training to failure vs. sub-failure) remains debated.
key_findings: One weekly resistance training session is sufficient to induce strength gains in beginners with <3 sets and loads below 50% 1RM for at least 8-12 weeks.
Untrained women demonstrated similar strength gains with one set versus two to four sets for the first 12 weeks of a 24-week program.
Meta-analysis by Ralston et al. found large magnitude effect size gains (exceeding 1.0) with single sets in novice and intermediate male trainees.
Multi-joint exercises induce similar or even larger effects than single-joint exercises for minimalist training.
Very low intensity activities such as prolonged static stretching (>10 min per muscle group) can improve strength and hypertrophy but require much longer session durations.
effect_size: Effect sizes exceeding 1.0 for single sets in untrained individuals (from Ralston et al. meta-analysis)
limitations: Narrative review design limits quantitative synthesis; high heterogeneity across studies in protocols and outcome measures; minimal research on single weekly sessions beyond 12 weeks; findings primarily apply to sedentary/untrained populations, not trained individuals.
